passed.title: to_string defaults to ISO with a space; use iso:strict for the T separator
passed.trap: Calling `Expr.dt.to_string()` with no format on a Datetime gives ISO date and time parts separated by a space, not by `T`. APIs that expect strict ISO 8601 may reject that output. Pass `'iso:strict'` to get the `T` separator, or give an explicit chrono format. `Expr.dt.strftime` is an alias of `Expr.dt.to_string` but requires a format. Duration columns cannot use strftime patterns at all; only `'iso'` and `'polars'` are supported for them.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
from datetime import datetime

df = pl.DataFrame({"ts": [datetime(2024, 5, 1, 8, 30)]})
print(df.select(
    default_iso=pl.col("ts").dt.to_string(),
    iso_strict=pl.col("ts").dt.to_string("iso:strict"),
    custom=pl.col("ts").dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M"),
).rows())

passed.title: replace_time_zone relabels the wall clock, convert_time_zone keeps the instant
passed.trap: `Expr.dt.replace_time_zone` keeps the wall-clock reading, attaches a new zone and ignores the original zone, so the underlying timestamp changes. `Expr.dt.convert_time_zone` keeps the same instant and only changes how it is displayed. Calling `Expr.dt.convert_time_zone` on a naive column treats the values as UTC, whatever your system zone is. To declare which zone naive data is in, call `Expr.dt.replace_time_zone` first, then `Expr.dt.convert_time_zone`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
from datetime import datetime

fmt = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M %z"
df = pl.DataFrame({"ts": [datetime(2024, 7, 1, 12, 0)]})
utc = df.with_columns(pl.col("ts").dt.replace_time_zone("UTC"))
out = utc.select(
    converted=pl.col("ts").dt.convert_time_zone("Europe/Amsterdam"),
    replaced=pl.col("ts").dt.replace_time_zone("Europe/Amsterdam"),
)
print(out.select(pl.all().dt.to_string(fmt)).rows())
# Different instants: epoch seconds differ by 7200
print(out.select(
    conv_s=pl.col("converted").dt.epoch("s"),
    repl_s=pl.col("replaced").dt.epoch("s"),
).rows())
# Naive input to convert_time_zone is treated as UTC (14:00 +0200)
naive_conv = pl.col("ts").dt.convert_time_zone("Europe/Amsterdam")
print(df.select(naive_conv.dt.to_string(fmt)).rows())
# Correct way to say naive data is local Amsterdam time (12:00 +0200)
local = pl.col("ts").dt.replace_time_zone("Europe/Amsterdam")
print(df.select(local.dt.to_string(fmt)).rows())

passed.title: Use replace_time_zone(None) instead of the deprecated dt.datetime
passed.trap: `Expr.dt.datetime` has been deprecated since 0.20.4 and emits a deprecation warning. Its job was to drop the time zone from a Datetime column, and `Expr.dt.replace_time_zone(None)` does the same thing. It keeps the wall-clock values and removes the zone, so use it in new code.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
import warnings
from datetime import datetime

df = pl.DataFrame(
    {"ts": [datetime(2024, 1, 1, 9, 30)]},
    schema={"ts": pl.Datetime(time_zone="UTC")},
)
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("error")
    try:
        df.select(pl.col("ts").dt.datetime())
    except Exception as e:
        print(str(type(e)).split("'")[1].split(".")[-1])

out = df.with_columns(naive=pl.col("ts").dt.replace_time_zone(None))
print(out.schema)
print(out.to_dicts())
passed.output:
DeprecationWarning
Schema({'ts': Datetime(time_unit='us', time_zone='UTC'), 'naive': Datetime(time_unit='us', time_zone=None)})
[{'ts': datetime.datetime(2024, 1, 1, 9, 30, tzinfo=zoneinfo.ZoneInfo(key='UTC')), 'naive': datetime.datetime(2024, 1, 1, 9, 30)}]

passed.title: epoch and timestamp default to microseconds, not Unix seconds
passed.trap: `Expr.dt.epoch()` and `Expr.dt.timestamp()` both default to `time_unit='us'`. Code that expects Unix seconds or nanoseconds will be off by a large factor. For Unix seconds, pass `Expr.dt.epoch(time_unit='s')`. `Expr.dt.timestamp` only accepts `'ns'`, `'us'` and `'ms'`, so use `Expr.dt.epoch` when you need seconds or days.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
from datetime import datetime

df = pl.DataFrame({"ts": [datetime(2001, 1, 1)]})
out = df.select(
    epoch_default_us=pl.col("ts").dt.epoch(),
    timestamp_default_us=pl.col("ts").dt.timestamp(),
    unix_seconds=pl.col("ts").dt.epoch(time_unit="s"),
    unix_days=pl.col("ts").dt.epoch(time_unit="d"),
    unix_ms=pl.col("ts").dt.timestamp("ms"),
)
print(out.to_dicts())

passed.title: second() drops fractions and the sub-second fields are not additive
passed.trap: `Expr.dt.second` returns an integer (Int8) by default, so 14.5 seconds comes back as 14. Pass `fractional=True` to get a Float64. `Expr.dt.millisecond`, `Expr.dt.microsecond` and `Expr.dt.nanosecond` each return the whole fractional part of the second in a different unit, so .5 s gives 500, 500000 and 500000000. Never add them together; pick the one unit you need.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
from datetime import datetime

df = pl.DataFrame({"ts": [datetime(2024, 1, 1, 0, 0, 14, 500_000)]})
out = df.select(
    sec=pl.col("ts").dt.second(),
    sec_frac=pl.col("ts").dt.second(fractional=True),
    ms=pl.col("ts").dt.millisecond(),
    us=pl.col("ts").dt.microsecond(),
    ns=pl.col("ts").dt.nanosecond(),
    wrong_total_us=pl.col("ts").dt.millisecond() * 1000
    + pl.col("ts").dt.microsecond(),
)
print(out.schema)
print(out.to_dicts())
passed.output:
Schema({'sec': Int8, 'sec_frac': Float64, 'ms': Int32, 'us': Int32, 'ns': Int32, 'wrong_total_us': Int32})
[{'sec': 14, 'sec_frac': 14.5, 'ms': 500, 'us': 500000, 'ns': 500000000, 'wrong_total_us': 1000000}]

passed.title: Use offset_by for calendar months and years, and remember 1m means minute
passed.trap: Adding a `timedelta` adds a fixed span of time, so adding 30 or 365 days drifts away from "one month later" or "one year later", especially across leap years. `Expr.dt.offset_by` understands calendar months and years. In its offset language `'1m'` means one minute and `'1mo'` means one calendar month, so writing `'1m'` for a month gives silently wrong results. A negative offset uses a single leading minus sign, for example `'-1y2mo'`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

df = pl.DataFrame({"d": [datetime(2024, 1, 15), datetime(2023, 3, 1)]})
out = df.with_columns(
    plus_30d=pl.col("d") + timedelta(days=30),
    plus_1mo=pl.col("d").dt.offset_by("1mo"),
    plus_365d=pl.col("d") + timedelta(days=365),
    plus_1y=pl.col("d").dt.offset_by("1y"),
    oops_1m_is_minute=pl.col("d").dt.offset_by("1m"),
    minus_1y2mo=pl.col("d").dt.offset_by("-1y2mo"),
)
for row in out.select(pl.all().dt.to_string("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")).to_dicts():
    print(row)

passed.title: dt.round goes to the nearest bucket boundary; use dt.truncate to floor
passed.trap: `Expr.dt.round` maps values in the first half of an interval to the start of the bucket and values in the second half to the end of the bucket, so 01:40 rounded to `'1h'` becomes 02:00. If you want every value floored to the start of its bucket (for example for hourly grouping keys), use `Expr.dt.truncate` instead. Also remember that `'1m'` is minutes and `'1mo'` is months in `every`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
from datetime import datetime

df = pl.DataFrame({"ts": [
    datetime(2024, 1, 1, 1, 20),
    datetime(2024, 1, 1, 1, 40),
]})
out = df.with_columns(
    rounded=pl.col("ts").dt.round("1h"),
    truncated=pl.col("ts").dt.truncate("1h"),
)
print(out.columns)
print(out.select(pl.all().dt.to_string("%H:%M")).rows())

passed.title: add_business_days raises on weekend start dates unless you set roll
passed.trap: `Expr.dt.add_business_days` defaults to `roll='raise'`, so the whole query fails if any start date falls on a non-business day. Pass `roll='forward'` or `roll='backward'` to say how such dates should move before counting. Use `Expr.dt.is_business_day` to find the offending rows first. Both `Expr.dt.add_business_days` and `Expr.dt.is_business_day` are marked unstable and may change without notice.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
from datetime import date

# 2020-01-04 is a Saturday, 2020-01-06 is a Monday
df = pl.DataFrame({"start": [date(2020, 1, 4), date(2020, 1, 6)]})
try:
    df.select(pl.col("start").dt.add_business_days(1))
except Exception as e:
    print(str(type(e)).split("'")[1].split(".")[-1])

out = df.with_columns(
    is_bday=pl.col("start").dt.is_business_day(),
    fwd=pl.col("start").dt.add_business_days(1, roll="forward"),
    back=pl.col("start").dt.add_business_days(1, roll="backward"),
)
for row in out.to_dicts():
    print(row)

verification.reason: The output shows the space and `T` separators, and the docstrings support the `strftime` alias, its required format and the Duration format restriction.
The output shows the 7200-second instant difference and naive values being converted as if UTC, matching both docstrings.
The output shows the DeprecationWarning and that `replace_time_zone(None)` keeps the wall clock, and the docstring gives the 0.20.4 deprecation.
The output confirms both functions default to microseconds, and the docstrings confirm `timestamp` accepts only ns, us and ms.
The schema and values show Int8 versus Float64 and the 500/500000/500000000 overlap, which makes summing them wrong.
The output shows the timedelta drift including the leap-day case, `'1m'` adding a minute and the `'-1y2mo'` result, all consistent with the docstring.
The output shows 01:40 rounding to 02:00 while truncate floors it to 01:00, matching the docstrings.
The output shows a ComputeError on the Saturday start date and the roll results, and the docstrings mark both APIs unstable.
